title: Should you switch lanes in traffic? The math says stay
description:
In stop-and-go traffic the next lane looks faster most of the time, even when it isn't. Say both lanes move in waves, a mile at 20 mph and a mile at 40, out of step with each other. Your slow mile takes 3 minutes and your fast mile only 90 seconds, so two thirds of the time you're the slower lane. But slow cars bunch up (60 a mile) and fast ones spread out (30 a mile): 30 cars pass you while you crawl, and you pass 30 back while you're moving. Same average speed, same arrival. Redelmeier and Tibshirani showed the illusion in Nature (1999): in their simulation the next lane looked faster even with equal average speeds, and 70% of driving students shown a video thought the next lane was faster when it was slightly slower.

Numbers checked in code (verify.py), including a 5,000-driver simulation and 100,000 random glances. Sources: ScienceDaily (30 Aug 1999) and University of Toronto Magazine on the Nature study.

The math behind real problems, twice a day. Subscribe and the next one finds you.

social_caption: The other lane always looks faster. In stop-and-go traffic it usually isn't: here's the counting that shows you get there at the same time.
facts_checked: Model: alternating 1-mile stretches at 20 and 40 mph, lanes out of step, same flow (1,200 cars/h): slow mile 3 min, fast mile 90 s, next lane faster 2/3 of the time; density 60 vs 30 cars a mile; 30 cars pass you, you pass 30; average 26.7 mph both lanes; CTA at 10 mph: 80% (verify.py, with a 5,000-driver simulation and 100,000 random glances)

Redelmeier & Tibshirani, Nature 401, 35 (2 Sept 1999): in computer models of congested roads the next lane appeared faster even if all lanes had the same average speed; 'Vehicles spread out when going fast and pack together when moving slowly'; a driver can pass many vehicles in a brief time but takes much longer to be overtaken by the same number (https://sciencedaily.com/releases/1999/08/990830184718.htm)

70 per cent of driving students shown a videotape from a moving vehicle believed the next lane was moving faster when it was actually slightly slower; Redelmeier, University of Toronto / Sunnybrook (https://magazine.utoronto.ca/leading-edge/perceptions-of-speed-study/)

beats.say: Stuck in traffic. Switch lanes, or stay put?
The other lane always seems faster. Mostly, it isn't. It just looks that way.
Your jam moves in waves: a mile at 20 miles an hour, then a mile at 40. The next lane too, out of step.
Your slow mile takes 3 minutes. The whole time, the next lane slides past you.
Your fast mile takes just 90 seconds. Now you pass them.
So who's winning? Count the cars.
Slow cars bunch up: 60 to a mile. Fast cars spread out: 30.
In your 3 slow minutes, 30 cars pass you. In your 90 fast seconds, you pass 30 back. A dead tie.
Same speed, same arrival. But for two thirds of your drive, you watch the other lane win.
In a Toronto study, 70% of driving students picked the next lane as faster. It was slightly slower.
So if your slow part were 10 miles an hour, how often would the other lane look faster?
